newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: Gulf Arabs raise U.S. vote on Jerusalem with Cohen.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Arabs raise U.S. vote on Jerusalem with Cohen.

text.p: Gulf Arab states angered by a U.S. vote on Jerusalem as Israel's undivided capital have raised the issue with visiting U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen, U.S. officials travelling with him said on Tuesday.

"I think that most of the nations in the region are concerned that the peace process has not been on track," Cohen said in response to a question about a House of Representatives resolution at a news conference in Bahrain before flying on to the United Arab Emirates.
The non-binding resolution, passed by a 406-17 vote last week, angered Arabs at a time when Israeli-Palestinian relations are in crisis over construction of a Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem.
Israel claims Jerusalem as its undivided capital but Palestinians regard the eastern part of the city as capital of a future Palestinian state.

"The resolution that was passed by the House would not contribute to getting the peace process back on track," Cohen told reporters in Bahrain. "And as I indicated before, the resolution does not reflect the administration's policy."
Saudi Arabia, Washington's most significant ally in the Gulf, on Monday described the vote as an obstacle to the Middle East peace process.
"Saudi Arabia has warned that the resolution is a violation of the foundations of peace in the region," a cabinet statement reported by the official Saudi Press Agency said.
It said King Fahd, who chaired Monday's weekly cabinet meeting, stressed that the resolution was likely to hamper efforts to rescue the peace process from deadlock.

UAE newspapers have joined a chorus of condemnation of the vote. Gulf Today said on Tuesday that to rake up the question of Jerusalem in the present atmosphere of turmoil among the Palestinians was to pour oil over a raging fire.
"Indeed, the massive tilt in favour of the Jewish state can only compromise the U.S. endeavour to mediate in the protracted Middle East crisis," it said.
"That is why the Arab world, including Saudi Arabia and the UAE, have been unanimous in their criticism of the House of Representatives."

The English-language daily urged the Clinton administration to stop Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in his tracks and tell the House of Representatives that its resolution compromised larger U.S. interests in the region.
"It must then quickly resume its honest broker's journey in the Middle East," it added.
